Gurman notes that although Apple and LG “worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand,” adding that “the South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support” and has sought regulatory approval in recent weeks.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.

It is worth noting that although these products are part of Apple’s broader push into the connected home, which is expected to expand next week with the introduction of its new smart home hub , an updated Apple TV , and a new HomePod mini , Bloomberg says that “the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.”

In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.

extraction.body: Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details. According to Bloomberg , Apple and LG have been working together to develop a series of connected home products that will complement Apple’s upcoming smart home hub, marking “a formal reboot of HomeKit.” That includes “a doorbell, thermostat, […] a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera,” says Bloomberg. Gurman notes that although Apple and LG “worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand,” adding that “the South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support” and has sought regulatory approval in recent weeks. This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps. It is worth noting that although these products are part of Apple’s broader push into the connected home, which is expected to expand next week with the introduction of its new smart home hub , an updated Apple TV , and a new HomePod mini , Bloomberg says that “the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.” In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories. That includes products labeled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early next year. The filings don’t mention Apple’s involvement. sources.title: Apple’s smart home push includes doorbell, lock, thermostat co-developed with LG - The Straits Times
passages: CUPERTINO, California – Apple’s upcoming push into smart home devices will include a doorbell, thermostat and other accessories developed through an unusual partnership with LG Electronics.
Many of the devices include support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth networks, as well as Thread and Matter, two smart home protocols embraced by Apple and its rivals in recent years.
The products developed with South Korea’s LG will also include a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera.
Nearly a decade ago, when Apple temporarily exited the external computer monitor market, it co-developed monitors with LG to work with the iPhone maker’s laptops.
The company also is selling its first smart lock outside of South Korea.
Apple has used this strategy before: It has discreetly worked with companies like Foxconn Technology Group’s Belkin and Logitech International SA to develop products that sell under other brands.
LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early 2027.
The filings do not mention Apple’s involvement.
The new Apple devices are set to be introduced on Oct 13.
Development of the LG accessories has lagged behind Apple’s own devices, and the products are not expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.

The company is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.

For Apple, the new home ecosystem and devices will mark a formal reboot of HomeKit, a platform it launched in 2014 that has gained little traction compared with offerings from Amazon.com and Alphabet’s Google.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories.
Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.
Spokespeople for Apple and LG declined to comment.
LG Display supplies displays for many Apple products, including screens for devices.

The products developed with South Korea’s LG will also include a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the undertaking is private. Though the two companies worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand. The South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support. This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps. Development of the LG accessories has lagged behind Apple’s own devices, and the products are not expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months. Spokespeople for Apple and LG declined to comment. In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organisations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories. That includes products labelled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early 2027. The filings do not mention Apple’s involvement. Many of the devices include support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth networks, as well as Thread and Matter, two smart home protocols embraced by Apple and its rivals in recent years. The door lock also supports UWB, or ultra-wideband capability, a feature that allows for auto-unlocking when users approach their door. For Apple, the new home ecosystem and devices will mark a formal reboot of HomeKit, a platform it launched in 2014 that has gained little traction compared with offerings from Amazon.com and Alphabet’s Google. Apple aims to use its smart home devices and Siri AI assistant to breathe new life into the category. The company is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported. For LG, a company better known for TVs and washing machines, the devices will mark its own smart home expansion. The line-up represents its first indoor camera in nearly a decade, as well as its first outdoor camera, thermostat, floodlight camera and doorbell in recent history. The company also is selling its first smart lock outside of South Korea. This would put Apple and LG in closer competition with Amazon’s Ring and Google’s Nest, which are firmly entrenched in the smart home. Each already offers similar devices that let customers keep tabs on every corner of their house and surrounding property. Amazon’s October Big Deal Days are underway (lasting through tomorrow night), and we spotted a ton of Apple products and accessories in the sale, ranging from laptops and headphones to desktops and more. Some of the deals are only for Prime members , but other retailers are often matching or beating Amazon’s prices, and we’ll continue to update our coverage as we spot those deals. If your sights are set beyond what Apple makes, our main roundup has over 100 of the best deals from October Prime Day, and we’re keeping it updated throughout the sale. The iPhone Air is Apple’s thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6mm, featuring a 6.5-inch ProMotion display, a 48MP fusion camera, and an 18MP front camera with Center Stage support. But its single rear camera and “meh” battery life mean it’s not for everyone. The iPhone 16E is the spiritual successor to the iPhone SE, bringing flagship-level performance for less than the standard 16. We really wish it included MagSafe for $599, but those upgrading from older iPhones will probably be satisfied with what’s included. Apple’s second-generation AirPods Max have excellent sound and ANC performance, but are only a minor upgrade from the older pair. Read our review . Powered by Apple’s new M5 chip, the latest MacBook Airs are more powerful than prior models and offer double the base storage (512GB). They also support faster wireless standards, specifically Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Read our review . The 15-inch Apple MacBook Air features improved performance and better connectivity than the previous generation, and better speakers than the 13-inch model. The seventh-gen iPad Mini comes with Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It’s also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi-Fi and USB-C speeds. Read our review . A slick 2-in-1 charger that can charge your magnet-friendly iPhone or Pixel at a relatively speedy pace. Its extra charging pad supports AirPods, the Apple Watch, and other Qi-ready accessories. Slap a recent iPhone onto this charging pad and it’ll charge at fast 25W speeds. It can also charge AirPods, and includes a cord and wall adapter. The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review. The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review . The M4-powered iPad Air excels at AI-powered tasks, and has great battery life, but the 60Hz screen feels underwhelming. Read our review . Apple’s entry-level iPad is an excellent tablet for casual use, even if it is getting a little long in the tooth. Its high-res screen is great for watching video, and its A16 processor is still fast enough to handle light games and productivity apps. Read our review . Apple’s recently-updated Mac Mini packs surprising performance into a small package, and the discount helps offset a generational price bump. Read our review . The newest generation of Apple Watch packs in a variety of upgrades, like faster charging and updated sensors, alongside new Siri and AI features. Read our review . Apple’s AirPods 4 are last-gen wireless earbuds, but they’re still great. The hard, plastic buds feature improved audio over the third-gen model, along with deep iOS integration and spatial audio with head tracking. Read our review . This Apple iPhone case features a woven fabric made from recycled polyester for a unique look and rugged protection. The Apple Pencil Pro arrives with new features like Find My support so you can find the stylus when it gets lost, as well as new creative capabilities like squeeze gestures and the “Barrel Roll” gyroscope. This keyboard for the iPad turns your tablet into a tiny laptop, and is detachable in case you’d rather just use the kickstand folio cover. This Speck case features specially designed grips that help prevent accidental drops, and is made from 50 percent recycled plastic. The Force Case from Casetify comes in a handful of trendy colors, and supports MagSafe accessories and chargers.

sources.title: SpaceX looks to raise $40bn to buy Nvidia chips in financing led by Apollo - Yahoo Finance
passages: Elon Musk's SpaceX is seeking to raise $40bn in a financing effort led by Apollo Global Management to purchase Nvidia chips as the AI and rocket group amplifies its bet on the chipmaker's advanced technology.
Apollo also led a $35bn chip financing deal in June for processors made by Nvidia rival Broadcom, marking the largest private credit transaction at the time.
SpaceX and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"We've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call in August, referring to Nvidia's cutting-edge AI platform.

In August, Nvidia announced that it was working with some of the largest firms on Wall Street on a $500bn funding platform , signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR.
It would also mark a win for Nvidia, as it contends with growing competition from chipmakers aiming to challenge its dominance in advanced semiconductors.

The consortium aims to create pools of third-party capital to finance the acquisition of Nvidia's chips and broader build-out of AI infrastructure at lower borrowing costs for its smaller clients, with Nvidia potentially backstopping up to 25 per cent of the chip value.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
SpaceX's financing plans underscore the vast sums that are being raised to pay for investments in data centres, chips and other infrastructure underpinning AI.

Investors who SpaceX has previously approached about financing its multibillion-dollar chip purchase said they only received a short two-page deal memo with pictures of outer space and an arrow pointing out that the company was going to build data centres "somewhere in the universe".
Apollo has made lending to high-grade companies a pillar of its $800bn credit business, leading multibillion-dollar financing transactions for groups such as Intel and Bayer.
Its life insurance and annuities affiliate Athene typically buys are a large portion of these offerings.
Insurance and pension funds would be able to buy SpaceX's debt due to its BBB credit rating, the second-lowest investment-grade ranking.
Such funds take much more limited positions in junk-rated notes.
SpaceX secured an investment-grade rating shortly after its $86bn initial public offering in June.
It sold $25bn in high-grade bonds less than two weeks later.
However, the bonds sold off in the following days due to concerns over its mounting debt and heavy capital expenditure.
Private capital group Apollo is expected to lead the deal and help sell the debt to a broad base of investors.
Bond group Pimco was among a small group of lenders in talks to fund the deal, the people said.
Musk's limited financial disclosures have kept some investors away from SpaceX debt in the past.

coreStoryFacts.text: Elon Musk's SpaceX is seeking to raise $40bn in a financing effort led by Apollo Global Management to purchase Nvidia chips as the AI and rocket group amplifies its bet on the chipmaker's advanced technology.
Apollo also led a $35bn chip financing deal in June for processors made by Nvidia rival Broadcom, marking the largest private credit transaction at the time.
SpaceX and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"We've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call in August, referring to Nvidia's cutting-edge AI platform.

In August, Nvidia announced that it was working with some of the largest firms on Wall Street on a $500bn funding platform , signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR.
It would also mark a win for Nvidia, as it contends with growing competition from chipmakers aiming to challenge its dominance in advanced semiconductors.

The consortium aims to create pools of third-party capital to finance the acquisition of Nvidia's chips and broader build-out of AI infrastructure at lower borrowing costs for its smaller clients, with Nvidia potentially backstopping up to 25 per cent of the chip value.

SpaceX's financing plans underscore the vast sums that are being raised to pay for investments in data centres, chips and other infrastructure underpinning AI.

Investors who SpaceX has previously approached about financing its multibillion-dollar chip purchase said they only received a short two-page deal memo with pictures of outer space and an arrow pointing out that the company was going to build data centres "somewhere in the universe".
Apollo has made lending to high-grade companies a pillar of its $800bn credit business, leading multibillion-dollar financing transactions for groups such as Intel and Bayer.
Its life insurance and annuities affiliate Athene typically buys are a large portion of these offerings.
Insurance and pension funds would be able to buy SpaceX's debt due to its BBB credit rating, the second-lowest investment-grade ranking.
Such funds take much more limited positions in junk-rated notes.
SpaceX secured an investment-grade rating shortly after its $86bn initial public offering in June.
It sold $25bn in high-grade bonds less than two weeks later.
However, the bonds sold off in the following days due to concerns over its mounting debt and heavy capital expenditure.
Private capital group Apollo is expected to lead the deal and help sell the debt to a broad base of investors.

SpaceX's financing plans underscore the vast sums that are being raised to pay for investments in data centres, chips and other infrastructure underpinning AI.

relevantPassages.text: SpaceX is seeking to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia artificial intelligence chips (more on NVDA here , and here ) in a financing led by Apollo Global Management, the Financial Times (gated, but some info is here ) reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The Elon Musk-led company plans to raise about $10 billion through bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt to fund the order, according to the report.
Apollo is expected to lead the deal and help place the debt with a broad range of investors.
The chips are intended for SpaceX's AI computing operations.
The company absorbed Musk's xAI before going public in June in a record initial public offering of around $86 billion, and it runs the Grok AI model through its Colossus data centers.
Musk has said SpaceX will use Nvidia hardware exclusively in those facilities and said last month that the Colossus 2 data center could more than double its Nvidia chip count by December.
SpaceX also rents out Colossus computing capacity to other AI developers, mainly Anthropic and Alphabet's Google.
The planned fundraising shows the scale of capital the AI boom now requires.
Morgan Stanley estimates AI infrastructure will need $1.5 trillion in external financing by 2028, even as lenders and investors grow more cautious about funding the expansion.
Nvidia itself partnered in August with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing platforms aimed at mobilising more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure.
SpaceX shares fell about 1% in extended trading after the report, while Nvidia gained about 0.5%.
SpaceX, Apollo and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and Pimco declined to comment, Reuters reported.

For Nvidia, a large debt-financed order from a customer committed to using its hardware exclusively supports the demand outlook, although the muted share reaction suggests much of that is already priced in.
SpaceX secures $40bn for Nvidia AI chips, a massive bet on AI compute.

Deutsche Bank says Australian households are absorbing RBA rate hikes better than expected, with a debt-to-asset ratio at its lowest since 1997, a view that cuts against RBA staff warnings of a wealth hit from falling house and AI stock prices.

passages: [LOS ANGELES] Elon Musk’s SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise US$40 billion of debt to buy chips from Nvidia, people familiar with the matter said, underscoring the insatiable demand among artificial intelligence developers for more computing power.
In September, Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by end-2026.
SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the report, falling as much as 1.8 per cent in New York, while Nvidia’s stock rose as much as 0.6 per cent.
Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure .
Tech companies and AI model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of US dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems.
Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley.

The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”.
SpaceX’s fundraising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said.

Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signalled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify towards this commitment.

In September, Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by end-2026.
SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the report, falling as much as 1.8 per cent in New York, while Nvidia’s stock rose as much as 0.6 per cent.
Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure .
Tech companies and AI model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of US dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems.
Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley.

The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”.
SpaceX’s fundraising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said.

Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Times’ report.
Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure.
In September , Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of 2026 .

The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR & Co. – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”.
SpaceX’s fund-raising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said.
Tech companies and artificial intelligence model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems.

Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signalled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify towards this commitment.

extraction.body: As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B , released with open weights. The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need. As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively. “Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.” Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September , which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon . Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture. One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior. Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques. Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads. As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.

“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”

Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September , which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon . Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.
One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.

Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.

Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

sources.title: Acurast brings real time AI decision model Laya to smartphone network
passages: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers.

According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation.

Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs.
More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company.
“By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said.
Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network.
Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response.
Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats.

“We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license.
Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text.
Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity.
Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.
For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed.
Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well.
Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs.

extraction.body: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers. Acurast has deployed open source Laya AI across its decentralized smartphone compute network. Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text. Acurast said decisions typically take around 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs without dedicated GPUs. More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company. According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation. Acurast brings Laya AI model to smartphone compute network Laya, developed by Convai Innovations under an Apache 2.0 license, is designed to make structured decisions instead of generating conversational responses. Given a defined state and a set of possible actions, the model evaluates the input and selects an option. Its open source repository describes three main decision formats covering choices between defined options, scoring against a set range and boolean decisions. The model uses a non autoregressive architecture, meaning it does not generate an answer token by token in the way large language models typically produce text. Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response. Acurast is using the model to demonstrate how such workloads can operate across commodity mobile hardware. Each decision in its deployment is processed on an Android smartphone connected to the network, according to the company. “By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said. “We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Its repository lists a 421 million parameter English checkpoint, alongside separate models for multilingual and typed decision workloads. Acurast has set up several live demonstrations to test the model across different types of decision based tasks. For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed. A Doom demonstration requires the model to make decisions around movement, aiming, shooting, collecting items and exploring the game environment. The model can classify emails as inbox messages, spam or phishing attempts and sort headlines into categories including news, satire, clickbait and manipulation. Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats. Users can submit their own letters, headlines, prompts and other inputs to the demonstrations and observe the decisions made by the model. Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well. The project’s repository says its general model performs poorly on some zero shot typed decision tests and recommends specializing the model for specific tasks. It advises keeping choice questions below roughly 20 options and recalibrating probabilities using application specific data. Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs. Work is distributed dynamically between devices participating in the network. Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity. The network uses Trusted Execution Environments built into modern smartphones to isolate workloads and protect data while computation takes place, according to Acurast. Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs. The company has previously applied the same model to blockchain infrastructure and other decentralized computing workloads. Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network. At the time, the network had more than 72,000 smartphones and had processed 256 million transactions. Acurast now says more than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the network, while the number of on chain transactions processed has passed 918 million. The model fits into a growing effort to use consumer devices for decentralized AI workloads. Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.

passages: As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B , released with open weights.

The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need.
As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.

“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”

Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September , which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon . Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.
One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.

Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.

Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

sources.title: Acurast brings real time AI decision model Laya to smartphone network
passages: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers.

According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation.

Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs.
More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company.
“By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said.
Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network.
Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response.
Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats.

“We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license.
Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text.
Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity.
Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.
For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed.
Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well.
Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs.

extraction.body: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers. Acurast has deployed open source Laya AI across its decentralized smartphone compute network. Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text. Acurast said decisions typically take around 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs without dedicated GPUs. More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company. According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation. Acurast brings Laya AI model to smartphone compute network Laya, developed by Convai Innovations under an Apache 2.0 license, is designed to make structured decisions instead of generating conversational responses. Given a defined state and a set of possible actions, the model evaluates the input and selects an option. Its open source repository describes three main decision formats covering choices between defined options, scoring against a set range and boolean decisions. The model uses a non autoregressive architecture, meaning it does not generate an answer token by token in the way large language models typically produce text. Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response. Acurast is using the model to demonstrate how such workloads can operate across commodity mobile hardware. Each decision in its deployment is processed on an Android smartphone connected to the network, according to the company. “By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said. “We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Its repository lists a 421 million parameter English checkpoint, alongside separate models for multilingual and typed decision workloads. Acurast has set up several live demonstrations to test the model across different types of decision based tasks. For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed. A Doom demonstration requires the model to make decisions around movement, aiming, shooting, collecting items and exploring the game environment. The model can classify emails as inbox messages, spam or phishing attempts and sort headlines into categories including news, satire, clickbait and manipulation. Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats. Users can submit their own letters, headlines, prompts and other inputs to the demonstrations and observe the decisions made by the model. Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well. The project’s repository says its general model performs poorly on some zero shot typed decision tests and recommends specializing the model for specific tasks. It advises keeping choice questions below roughly 20 options and recalibrating probabilities using application specific data. Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs. Work is distributed dynamically between devices participating in the network. Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity. The network uses Trusted Execution Environments built into modern smartphones to isolate workloads and protect data while computation takes place, according to Acurast. Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs. The company has previously applied the same model to blockchain infrastructure and other decentralized computing workloads. Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network. At the time, the network had more than 72,000 smartphones and had processed 256 million transactions. Acurast now says more than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the network, while the number of on chain transactions processed has passed 918 million. The model fits into a growing effort to use consumer devices for decentralized AI workloads. Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.

It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar .
The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

extraction.body: Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer. But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job. Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog. However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity. What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction. For instance, TechCrunch has seen a han d ful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ( NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.) But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences. The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out. It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into. To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post. This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology. For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests. Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.” “While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained. United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.) Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp , eBay , Zillow , Pizza Hut , Adidas , and various airlines . Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased . A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them. Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program . That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp. eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training. Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication. One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads. However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones. Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents. Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs. Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.
Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication.

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

extraction.body: Ninety-seven percent of top websites aren’t ready for AI agents, according to research from BrightEdge, an AI-powered organic search provider. But these agents are here, and they are banging on your website’s door. Is there a way to let them in without rebuilding your website to meet their needs? BrightEdge says yes, and it has it. BrightEdge says that for every 100 visits a site receives from human organic search, it receives, on average, 88 from AI agents, the bulk of which are from OpenAI. AI Agents have become digital assistants that help people get the information they need, including researching products, comparing options, and checking product availability. These agents don’t just hit your website once; instead, they often make multiple trips to your site to get everything they need for the end user. Says BrightEdge: For digital marketers, that number [95% of agent interactions come from OpenAI] has a practical implication that goes beyond strategy. If you haven't already had conversations with your IT, dev, or ops teams about AI agents, there's a good chance those agents are currently being treated the same as any other bot -- meaning they may be throttled, blocked, or otherwise restricted from reaching your content. The systems that control this sit outside of marketing's hands, and closing that gap sooner rather than later is no longer optional. Your website needs to support these agents. You can’t block them; they are your window to get found in AI search or to help a ChatGPT user (or other AI assistant) answer questions about your brand and products. But you also don’t necessarily want them to come to your website and take forever to find the information they need. Agents work best with simplicity. They like structure - like Markdown (a lightweight, structured text format that strips away much of the presentation and scripting of a normal web page). And your website is not written in Markdown. BrightEdge says that AI agents are creating a “second web.” The second web is a new layer of access that creates a second audience for your content. How well you create that second web (and how you do it) affects the quality of the interactions between agents and your content. From June 2025 to June 2026, BrightEdge analyzed ChatGPT recommendations across nine industries. It found that ChatGPT researched more but recommended brands less. As Jim Yu, CEO and co-founder of BrightEdge, notes: AI agents are getting dramatically better at doing the work people once had to do themselves.They are researching, comparing and taking action on our behalf, making the point of interaction between an agent and a brand increasingly critical. The companies that can understand and optimize those interactions will have a significant advantage as this second audience grows. While it is important to ensure agents can get the right information, it’s not necessarily critical that information is delivered in Markdown format. For agents that specifically request it, yes, it needs to be available, but most agents can read a traditional web page fine, as long as it’s structured properly. In fact, Profound did an experiment to see if serving Markdown to agents improved a brand’s visibility in AI search. It looked at 381 pages across six websites, with half the pages serving HTML and half serving Markdown to AI agents.Here’s what it found: At first glance, the Markdown group looks slightly ahead: one more median visit per page, about 16% higher on average. But here's the catch: the median page (your typical page) only got one extra visit. The 16% mean difference is driven almost entirely by high-traffic pages in the tail of the distribution, pages that were already getting lots of bot attention saw modest gains, while the median page saw almost nothing. [..] Put simply: we can't say with confidence that Markdown actually drove more traffic. There’s more to supporting AI agents than implementing a schema, but that’s what most brands are doing today, says BrightEdge. Very few are taking the next step of serving content specially designed to support agent queries. That being said, Search Engine Optimization (SEO) tool providers are giving brands the tools they need to support AI agents, including BrightEdge. Here are a couple of them. Agent Edge looks for agent requests at the Content Delivery Network (CDN) layer. When it gets an agent request, it serves content to the agent in Markdown, reducing the number of tokens an agent uses. The Markdown versions are copies of the HTML web pages with all the extra stuff taken out (like navigation, JavaScript, and so on). Marketers have a dashboard where they can select the web pages they want converted to Markdown, and Agent Edge will create the Markdown version (marketers can make edits as well). BrightEdge goes further, though, because Agent Edge can use BrightEdge Intelligence to anticipate follow-on questions the agent is likely to ask and build on the initial content with those answers. Enriching the response with additional important information means the agent doesn’t have to come back and request more information. What’s nice about BrightEdge is that you get SEO, AI search, and agent interactions in one platform, allowing you to see and optimize holistically across all three. seoClarity also tracks AI agents and delivers content optimized as Markdown. Like BrightEdge, it is implemented at the CDN layer, intercepting all requests and delivering Markdown if an agent requests it (it’s called HTTP Content Negotiation). Brands can select which web pages to convert to Markdown and approve the Markdown version. Both the HTML and Markdown versions of a web page share the same canonical URL, making it easy to track and analyze traffic, with full auditability and logging. Cloudflare isn’t an SEO provider; it is an internet infrastructure and security company. A CDN is one of the products it provides. It also uses HTTP Content Negotiation, so when an agent sends a request and asks for a Markdown response, Cloudflare converts the web page in real time at the source and delivers it to the agent. To help brands learn how much Markdown is being delivered, Cloudflare added a content type to its Radar product, allowing marketers to see AI bot and crawler traffic. The more tools we have that help brands understand how to get found in AI search, the better. But marketers need to be careful and ask lots of questions about how features work and what results they can expect. And tool providers need to prove why they work the way they do. BrightEdge can track how AI agents interact with brands, what those agents are trying to access, and how that behavior is changing. That means they can show a brand the before-and-after of implementing Agent Edge. This is the kind of information brands need from their tool providers to know their investment is warranted. diginomica and the diginomica logo are trademarks of diginomica Limited. © Diginomica Limited and its licensors 2013- 2026

Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased . A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them. Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program . That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp. eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training. Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication. One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads. However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones. Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents. Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs. Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

passages: There’s more to supporting AI agents than implementing a schema, but that’s what most brands are doing today, says BrightEdge.
Very few are taking the next step of serving content specially designed to support agent queries.
That being said, Search Engine Optimization (SEO) tool providers are giving brands the tools they need to support AI agents, including BrightEdge.
These agents don’t just hit your website once; instead, they often make multiple trips to your site to get everything they need for the end user.
Ninety-seven percent of top websites aren’t ready for AI agents, according to research from BrightEdge, an AI-powered organic search provider.
Is there a way to let them in without rebuilding your website to meet their needs?

AI agents are getting dramatically better at doing the work people once had to do themselves.They are researching, comparing and taking action on our behalf, making the point of interaction between an agent and a brand increasingly critical.

extraction.body: Ninety-seven percent of top websites aren’t ready for AI agents, according to research from BrightEdge, an AI-powered organic search provider. But these agents are here, and they are banging on your website’s door. Is there a way to let them in without rebuilding your website to meet their needs? BrightEdge says yes, and it has it. BrightEdge says that for every 100 visits a site receives from human organic search, it receives, on average, 88 from AI agents, the bulk of which are from OpenAI. AI Agents have become digital assistants that help people get the information they need, including researching products, comparing options, and checking product availability. These agents don’t just hit your website once; instead, they often make multiple trips to your site to get everything they need for the end user. Says BrightEdge: For digital marketers, that number [95% of agent interactions come from OpenAI] has a practical implication that goes beyond strategy. If you haven't already had conversations with your IT, dev, or ops teams about AI agents, there's a good chance those agents are currently being treated the same as any other bot -- meaning they may be throttled, blocked, or otherwise restricted from reaching your content. The systems that control this sit outside of marketing's hands, and closing that gap sooner rather than later is no longer optional. Your website needs to support these agents. You can’t block them; they are your window to get found in AI search or to help a ChatGPT user (or other AI assistant) answer questions about your brand and products. But you also don’t necessarily want them to come to your website and take forever to find the information they need. Agents work best with simplicity. They like structure - like Markdown (a lightweight, structured text format that strips away much of the presentation and scripting of a normal web page). And your website is not written in Markdown. BrightEdge says that AI agents are creating a “second web.” The second web is a new layer of access that creates a second audience for your content. How well you create that second web (and how you do it) affects the quality of the interactions between agents and your content. From June 2025 to June 2026, BrightEdge analyzed ChatGPT recommendations across nine industries. It found that ChatGPT researched more but recommended brands less. As Jim Yu, CEO and co-founder of BrightEdge, notes: AI agents are getting dramatically better at doing the work people once had to do themselves.They are researching, comparing and taking action on our behalf, making the point of interaction between an agent and a brand increasingly critical. The companies that can understand and optimize those interactions will have a significant advantage as this second audience grows. While it is important to ensure agents can get the right information, it’s not necessarily critical that information is delivered in Markdown format. For agents that specifically request it, yes, it needs to be available, but most agents can read a traditional web page fine, as long as it’s structured properly. In fact, Profound did an experiment to see if serving Markdown to agents improved a brand’s visibility in AI search. It looked at 381 pages across six websites, with half the pages serving HTML and half serving Markdown to AI agents.Here’s what it found: At first glance, the Markdown group looks slightly ahead: one more median visit per page, about 16% higher on average. But here's the catch: the median page (your typical page) only got one extra visit. The 16% mean difference is driven almost entirely by high-traffic pages in the tail of the distribution, pages that were already getting lots of bot attention saw modest gains, while the median page saw almost nothing. [..] Put simply: we can't say with confidence that Markdown actually drove more traffic. There’s more to supporting AI agents than implementing a schema, but that’s what most brands are doing today, says BrightEdge. Very few are taking the next step of serving content specially designed to support agent queries. That being said, Search Engine Optimization (SEO) tool providers are giving brands the tools they need to support AI agents, including BrightEdge. Here are a couple of them. Agent Edge looks for agent requests at the Content Delivery Network (CDN) layer. When it gets an agent request, it serves content to the agent in Markdown, reducing the number of tokens an agent uses. The Markdown versions are copies of the HTML web pages with all the extra stuff taken out (like navigation, JavaScript, and so on). Marketers have a dashboard where they can select the web pages they want converted to Markdown, and Agent Edge will create the Markdown version (marketers can make edits as well). BrightEdge goes further, though, because Agent Edge can use BrightEdge Intelligence to anticipate follow-on questions the agent is likely to ask and build on the initial content with those answers. Enriching the response with additional important information means the agent doesn’t have to come back and request more information. What’s nice about BrightEdge is that you get SEO, AI search, and agent interactions in one platform, allowing you to see and optimize holistically across all three. seoClarity also tracks AI agents and delivers content optimized as Markdown. Like BrightEdge, it is implemented at the CDN layer, intercepting all requests and delivering Markdown if an agent requests it (it’s called HTTP Content Negotiation). Brands can select which web pages to convert to Markdown and approve the Markdown version. Both the HTML and Markdown versions of a web page share the same canonical URL, making it easy to track and analyze traffic, with full auditability and logging. Cloudflare isn’t an SEO provider; it is an internet infrastructure and security company. A CDN is one of the products it provides. It also uses HTTP Content Negotiation, so when an agent sends a request and asks for a Markdown response, Cloudflare converts the web page in real time at the source and delivers it to the agent. To help brands learn how much Markdown is being delivered, Cloudflare added a content type to its Radar product, allowing marketers to see AI bot and crawler traffic. The more tools we have that help brands understand how to get found in AI search, the better. But marketers need to be careful and ask lots of questions about how features work and what results they can expect. And tool providers need to prove why they work the way they do. BrightEdge can track how AI agents interact with brands, what those agents are trying to access, and how that behavior is changing. That means they can show a brand the before-and-after of implementing Agent Edge. This is the kind of information brands need from their tool providers to know their investment is warranted. diginomica and the diginomica logo are trademarks of diginomica Limited. © Diginomica Limited and its licensors 2013- 2026

Photo: Tia Dufour / U.S. Department of Homeland Security / Public Domain (The Center Square) - The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has purchased more California properties for the purpose of using them as detention centers. The latest transaction involves the Adelanto ICE Processing Center and Desert View Annex. The facilities are in Adelanto, a city in Southern California's San Bernardino County. They were purchased from the private prison corporation GEO Group for $950 million. Adelanto ICE Processing Center is one name for two properties: the Adelanto West ICE Processing Center (1,280 beds) and the Adelanto East ICE Processing Center (660 beds). Desert View Annex has 704 beds. GEO Group will continue to manage the daily operations under long-term contracts. That is the same deal that private prison operator CoreCivic got in July when it sold two Southern California immigration detention centers to the federal government for $1.5 billion. “We are pleased with the completion of these important asset sales to the U.S. federal government, and we look forward to continuing to provide high-quality secure support services under our existing long-term contracts with ICE,” George C. Zoley, Chairman, CEO, and founder of GEO Group, said this week in a press release . In total, DHS has purchased five properties in California this year.
